text: Domenico Lino Morichini (23 September 1773 – 19 November 1836) was an Italian physician and chemist who first identified fluorine in teeth, initially in a fossilized elephant tooth and later in human teeth. He also reported that steel could be magnetized by light rays, an observation that inspired experimental research. Born in Civita d'Antino, L'Aquila, to farmer Anselmo and Domitilla Moratti, Morichini was educated in Sora and later in Rome, where he earned a medical degree in 1792 and became a physician at the Santo Spirito hospital. He contributed to public health and delivered lectures on chemistry at the University of Rome. He advocated for Lavoisier's theory of combustion involving oxygen, rejecting the outdated phlogiston theory. During the new Roman Republic established in 1798, Morichini gained influence, though the republic collapsed in 1799; he was subsequently reinstated by Pope Pius VII as a professor at the University of Sapienza, a position he held until 1833. In 1802, he analyzed fossil elephant teeth and demonstrated the presence of fluorine through chemical analysis, producing hydrogen fluoride that corroded glass and reacting it with lime to form calcium fluoride, which he found to have the same properties as fluorspar. In 1812, Morichini asserted that iron could be magnetized by ultraviolet solar rays, a claim that drew attention from scientists such as Ampere and Faraday. Numerous individuals replicated the experiment, with some confirming the results—including Humphry Davy (a patient of Morichini in 1828), Georges Cuvier, Andreas von Baumgartner, and Mary Somerville—while others remained skeptical. After retiring, Morichini fell ill, suffered a stroke, and died in Rome. His wife, Cecilia Calidi (married in 1804), and seven children outlived him, one of whom became Cardinal Carlo Luigi Morichini.
